title: Hazel and the Bell
premise: Folklorist Jude Amberdale arrives in the drowned-hollow village of Wrenlow to record a lullaby that locals will sing only once, never twice — because the second singing wakes the Bell, an entity that counts its listeners and claims them one by one. When Jude's rented cottage mirrors begin lagging a second behind reality, they realize the Bell has already begun counting their family, who arrived with them seeking a quiet season of recovery. To save them, Jude must learn why the village sings once and falls silent, uncovering that the Bell was once a person the villagers sacrificed to stop a plague — and that it only wants someone to remember its name. In the end Jude survives by refusing both loyalty to the village's silence and the truth's easy cruelty: they give the Bell not a name but a song of its own, sung once, freely, breaking the count at the cost of every mirror in the world going dark for one full minute.
about_author: Quentin Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former archivist of parish records who spent a decade cataloguing funeral bells across coastal England before turning to fiction. They write horror rooted in folk custom, insisting that the scariest things are the ones villages agree not to mention.

chapters.title: The Song You Sing Once
chapters.summary: Jude Amberdale, POV. Arriving in Wrenlow on a rain-slicked afternoon, Jude interviews innkeeper Maren Cobb about the forbidden lullaby; Maren sings four lines, then goes white and refuses more. Emotional beat: professional curiosity curdling into unease as three patrons leave the pub mid-recording without a word.

chapters.title: Hollow House
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. The family moves into Hollow House, a cottage above the flooded quarry; spouse El and daughter Wren settle in while Jude catalogs local bell-lore. Beat: domestic warmth undercut when Wren hums the four recorded lines and every dog in the village stops barking at once.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Jude's POV, night. The bathroom mirror reflects Jude raising a hand a full second after they do. Testing other mirrors confirms the lag is growing. Beat: rationalist denial cracking into dread as Jude measures the delay with a metronome app and gets an impossible result — the lag is shortening.

chapters.title: The Counting House
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. She visits Hollow House uninvited, sees the lagging mirror, and tells the story she swore off telling: in 1843 the village rang a living man inside the church bell to end the fever, and he has been counting his hearers ever since. Beat: guilt, because Maren sang for Jude knowing what it might start.

chapters.title: Wren Hums
chapters.summary: Alternating Jude and Wren POVs. Wren, sleepwalking, hums the lullaby complete — all eight verses she couldn't have learned. The mirrors now show rooms no one is standing in. Beat: parental terror as Jude realizes the count includes their daughter, and the number being counted down is unknown.

chapters.title: Vestry Records
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. In the church vestry, Jude finds the 1843 ledger: the sacrificed man's name torn out of every page, replaced by a burn mark shaped like a clapper. Beat: the folklorist's thrill of discovery shadowed by the realization that erasing the name may be what keeps the Bell hungry.

chapters.title: The Lag Reaches Three
chapters.summary: El's POV. El, skeptical like Jude once was, films the kitchen mirror; the reflection shows El still sitting when real El stands. That night the reflection waves first. Beat: a skeptic's quiet collapse, and the marriage strain of El blaming Jude's recording for bringing this home.

chapters.title: What the Drowned Quarry Keeps
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Diving the flooded quarry with villager Tam Osgood, Jude finds the original bell, sunk in 1901, its bronze skin covered in scratched tally marks — thousands, still wet. Beat: awe tipping into horror when Tam counts the newest marks and says, 'That's us. It started counting us the day you came.'

chapters.title: The Village Refuses
chapters.summary: Multiple village POVs in interlocking vignettes. Jude begs the parish council for the ritual of containment; they refuse, some out of fear, some because their own ancestors' names are in the ledger. Beat: loneliness — the theme of loyalty vs. truth made civic, as the village chooses silence over saving outsiders.

chapters.title: Reflections Without Faces
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren sees figures in the mirrors now: villagers from the ledger era, faceless, mouthing a name. One presses a hand to the glass from the wrong side. Beat: eerie tenderness — Wren, unlike the adults, isn't afraid of them; she thinks they're lonely.

chapters.title: El Goes Missing for Six Hours
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. El vanishes between one tick of the clock and the next, returning with quarry water in their lungs and no memory, speaking in a cadence that isn't theirs. Beat: grief and helplessness — the price of survival becoming literal, paid in pieces of the people Jude loves.

chapters.title: The Ninth Verse
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren confesses there is a ninth verse, sung only by the man in the bell, which she heard once through her grandmother's wall. She teaches it to Jude against every vow she has. Beat: redemption offered too late to be simple — Maren's loyalty finally outweighing her fear.

chapters.title: Countdown in Bronze
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. The tallies on the sunken bell appear now on Hollow House's windows, condensing from the inside. The count stands at nine marks. Jude works out the arithmetic: nine days, or fewer if anyone else hears the song. Beat: cold clarity — the horror becomes a deadline.

chapters.title: Leaving Is Not Escaping
chapters.summary: El's POV. The family flees to Jude's sister's city flat; the mirrors there lag within hours. The Bell is not bound to Wrenlow — it is bound to the counted. Beat: despair and a hard decision — running is survival, but it dooms whoever they live near next.

chapters.title: Tam's Bargain
chapters.summary: Tam Osgood's POV. Tam offers himself: a villager born of ledger blood, willing to take the family's place in the count. Jude refuses to let him. Beat: the ethics of sacrifice interrogated — accepting Tam would be survival bought with someone else's loyalty.

chapters.title: The Name Under the Burn
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Using raking light and graphite, Jude recovers the burned name from the vestry ledger: Aldous Merrow, bell-founder, who volunteered so his children wouldn't be taken — and whose children were taken anyway. Beat: fury at the village's founding lie, and the first hint the Bell wants witness, not worship.

chapters.title: Merrow's Children
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, dreamlike. In the mirror-world Wren meets two faceless children who lead her to the bell itself, hanging in a reflection of the old church. They show her the ninth verse written in condensation. Beat: innocence as bridge — the child sees what adults cannot, that the monsters are mourners.

chapters.title: The Night of Eight Marks
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. The eighth mark appears; the house's clocks all strike though none are wound. El, half-claimed, begs Jude to let them go rather than watch them become something else. Beat: the darkest hour — love versus truth, each demanding the opposite choice.

chapters.title: Into the Reflection
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Jude steps through the lagging mirror into the reflected church, carrying the recovered name and the ninth verse, leaving Wren instructions in case they don't return. Beat: resolve — the folklorist finally believes, and belief here means walking toward the sound.

chapters.title: The Bell Remembers Its Name
chapters.summary: Jude's POV inside the mirror-world. Jude speaks Aldous Merrow's name aloud and sings the ninth verse back to him — his own words, witnessed at last. The count shatters; the faceless regain their faces. Beat: catharsis — the monster was a mourner, and being remembered is the only exorcism.

chapters.title: One Minute Dark
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs worldwide, brief. Every mirror on earth goes black for sixty seconds; in Wrenlow, the family holds hands in a house with no reflections, listening to a single free bell-note. Beat: awe and release — the price of survival paid collectively, briefly, and survivably.

chapters.title: The Song Sung Twice
chapters.summary: Jude's POV, epilogue. Months later, Jude publishes the ballad complete, all nine verses, under Merrow's name as co-author. In Wrenlow, Maren sings it twice at the restored church, and nothing happens except that people stay to listen. Final beat: quiet hope — truth, told fully and credited honestly, ends what silence perpetuated.
